original_question: Let Sigma be the set of all triples S of points in the Euclidean plane for which there exist geodesic multinets with exactly three unbalanced vertices located at S and with arbitrarily many balanced vertices. Is Sigma a measure-zero subset of (R^2)^3?
target_in_paper: Problem 3.1.3 in §3.1 of the paper: the open question asking whether the set Σ of triples of points in the Euclidean plane that support geodesic multinets with three unbalanced vertices and arbitrarily many balanced vertices has measure zero in (R^2)^3. It is posed immediately after Example 3.1.1 and Theorem 3.1.2. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the right official target, keeps the ambient space as the Euclidean plane, correctly asks about geodesic multinets rather than geodesic nets, keeps the condition of three unbalanced vertices at the prescribed triple, keeps the quantifier about arbitrarily many balanced vertices, and asks exactly the paper’s measure-zero question in (R^2)^3. So it is already very close to Problem 3.1.3. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, it should define a geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane: a finite multigraph in R^2 whose edges are straight-line segments with positive integer multiplicities, where edges may intersect or self-intersect, and where at each balanced vertex the multiplicity-weighted sum of outgoing unit tangent vectors is zero. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
It should make the paper’s standing conventions explicit: only connected geodesic (multi)nets are considered. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
It should include the convention that degree-2 balanced vertices are suppressed, so the intended balanced vertices are taken to have degree at least 3. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
It should include the convention that edges between unbalanced vertices are excluded. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

It should clarify the quantifier in “arbitrarily many balanced vertices” as: for every N in the natural numbers, there exists such a geodesic multinet with at least N balanced vertices. The paper leaves this quantifier implicit. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

It should clarify that, because the paper places Σ inside (R^2)^3, the clean stand-alone formulation is in terms of ordered triples S=(p1,p2,p3) in (R^2)^3. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

It should spell out that “measure zero in (R^2)^3” means Lebesgue measure zero in the 6-dimensional parameter space of triples; this is standard but implicit in the paper’s wording. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

It should avoid importing neighboring restrictions not present in Problem 3.1.3, such as bounded edge multiplicities; that is the separate Problem 3.1.4. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
refined_question: Let Σ ⊂ (R^2)^3 be the set of ordered triples S=(p1,p2,p3) such that, under the paper’s standing conventions, for every N∈N there exists a finite connected geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane whose unbalanced vertices are exactly p1,p2,p3, whose edges are straight-line segments carrying positive integer multiplicities, whose edges are allowed to intersect or self-intersect, whose balanced vertices satisfy the multiplicity-weighted balancing condition (the sum of outgoing unit tangent vectors, counted with multiplicity, is zero at each balanced vertex), whose balanced vertices have degree at least 3, which has no edge joining two unbalanced vertices, and which has at least N balanced vertices. Must Σ have Lebesgue measure zero in (R^2)^3? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
justification: The draft is trying to capture Problem 3.1.3, not a broader neighboring problem. Example 3.1.1 gives a family of geodesic multinets with three unbalanced vertices and arbitrarily many balanced vertices, but only for a very restricted family of triples, which the authors explicitly say has measure zero among triangles in the plane. Theorem 3.1.2 then shows extreme rigidity for actual geodesic nets with three unbalanced vertices in the Euclidean plane. Problem 3.1.3 asks whether the triples supporting such multinets are always confined to a measure-zero subset of (R^2)^3. So the right refinement is to keep the exact multinet/three-unbalanced-vertices/measure-zero scope while making the paper’s definitions and conventions explicit, and not to drift into Problem 3.1.4, classification, or higher-boundary-vertex variants. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
